## When information stops flowing {.hook background-color="#FAF7F2"}

In 1932 the spread between risky and safe borrowing went from **2%** to nearly
**8%**. In late 2008 it passed **500 basis points**.

::: incremental
-   In neither case was anything physical destroyed. The factories, the workers
    and the ideas were all still there the following morning.
-   What broke was the ability to tell a good borrower from a bad one — the
    exact problem we named last session.
-   A financial crisis is an **information** event. That is why this chapter
    follows directly from the last one, and why regulation takes the shape it
    does.
:::

::: notes
Open on the two numbers and let them sit before explaining anything.

Two per cent to eight in 1932. Over five hundred basis points in 2008. Those are
the prices of borrowing for anyone who was not unimpeachable.

*[reveal the first bullet]*

Nothing was destroyed. No factory burned down. The same people turned up to work
with the same skills and the same machines.

*[ask]* So what exactly was the problem?

Let them try. Steer towards: nobody could tell who was solvent.

*[reveal the second and third bullets]*

Last session we called that adverse selection and moral hazard, and treated it
as a reason intermediaries exist. This session it is the engine of collapse -
the same mechanism, turned up until the system stops.

Say the through-line for the whole chapter now, because everything hangs on it:
every piece of regulation in this session is an attempt to fix an information
problem, and every one of them creates a new incentive problem of its own.
:::

## Where we are {.center}

The last two sessions built the institutions. This one asks what happens when
they fail, and what is done about it.

# 1 · Financial crisis {.divider .center background-color="#06302F"}

## 1 · The characteristics

A functioning financial system is critical to a robust economy, and **agency
theory** — the study of both moral hazard and adverse selection — is the basis
for understanding and defining a financial crisis.

::: incremental
-   Asymmetric information creates **barriers** between savers and firms with
    productive investment opportunities.
-   A financial crisis occurs when information flows in financial markets
    experience a **particularly large disruption**.
-   Financial markets may stop functioning completely. Crises usually proceed in
    **two or three stages** to hit countries.
:::

::: notes
This is the definition the whole chapter runs on, so make them say it rather
than read it.

*[ask]* Last session, what stood between a saver and a firm with a good idea?

Asymmetric information. The saver cannot tell a good borrower from a bad one, so
they will not lend, or will not lend cheaply.

*[reveal the second bullet]*

Now the definition. A financial crisis is not a fall in prices, and it is not a
recession. It is a particularly large disruption to information flows.

*[ask]* Why does that definition matter more than a definition about prices?

Because it tells you where to look for the cause and what a remedy has to do.
Prices falling is a symptom. If the problem were prices, the cure would be to
support prices; since the problem is information, the cure has to restore the
ability to tell who is solvent. That is the logic behind every regulation in
sections five to seven.
:::

## 1 · Stage one of initiation: credit boom

A crisis can begin with **mismanagement of financial liberalisation or
innovation** — the elimination of restrictions, or the introduction of new types
of loans or other financial products.

::: incremental
-   It can lead to a **credit boom**, where risk management is lacking.
-   Government safety nets **weaken the incentive** to manage risk: depositors
    ignore bank risk-taking.
-   Loan losses accrue and asset values fall, reducing capital.
-   Institutions cut back lending — **deleveraging** — and bank funding falls
    too.
-   As institutions cut back, **nobody is left to evaluate firms**. The system
    loses its primary institution for addressing adverse selection and moral
    hazard, and spending contracts as loans become scarce.
:::

::: notes
Five bullets, revealed one at a time, and the last is the one that matters.

*[the first two]*

Liberalisation or innovation, then a credit boom nobody is managing the risk of.
And note the second bullet, because it is the chapter arriving early: the safety
net that protects depositors also stops them caring what the bank does. We come
back to that in section five.

*[the middle two]*

Losses, falling asset values, falling capital, and then deleveraging - selling
assets and cutting lending to rebuild the ratio.

*[the last one - slow down]*

This is the sentence to get them to write. As institutions cut back on lending,
nobody is left to evaluate firms. The system has lost the very institution whose
job was to tell good borrowers from bad.

*[ask]* So what happens to a sound firm that needs to borrow at that moment?

It cannot. Not because it is unsound, but because the machinery for proving
soundness has stopped.
:::

## 1 · Stage one of initiation: asset prices and uncertainty

:::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
**An asset-price boom and bust**

-   A pricing **bubble** starts, where asset values exceed their fundamental
    values.
-   When the bubble bursts and prices fall, corporate **net worth falls** too.
    Moral hazard increases, as firms have little left to lose.
-   Financial institutions also see a fall in their assets, leading again to
    **deleveraging**.
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**An increase in uncertainty**

-   Periods of high uncertainty can lead to crises — a stock market crash, or
    the failure of a major financial institution.
-   **1857**, when the Ohio Life Insurance & Trust Company failed.
-   **2008**, when AIG, Bear Stearns and Lehman Brothers failed.
-   With information hard to come by, moral hazard and adverse selection worsen,
    reducing lending and economic activity.
:::
::::

::: notes
Two more routes into the same stage. Both columns end in the same place, so say
that explicitly.

*[the left column]*

A bubble, then a bust. The part worth drawing out is the middle bullet: when net
worth falls, moral hazard rises, because a firm with nothing left to lose has
every reason to gamble. That is moral hazard in debt from last session, arriving
as a macroeconomic event.

*[the right column]*

Uncertainty. Two examples separated by a hundred and fifty years, and the same
mechanism in both: when a large institution fails, nobody is sure who else is
exposed, so lending to everybody stops.

*[ask]* Three different triggers. What do all three have in common?

They all end by making information worse. That is why the chapter treats them as
one phenomenon rather than three.
:::

## 1 · Stage two of banking crisis

::: incremental
-   Deteriorating balance sheets lead financial institutions into **insolvency**.
-   If severe enough, these factors can lead to a **bank panic**.
-   Panics occur when depositors are unsure which banks are insolvent, causing
    **all** depositors to withdraw **all** funds immediately.
-   As cash balances fall, institutions must sell assets quickly, further
    deteriorating their balance sheets.
-   Adverse selection and moral hazard become severe — and it takes **years**
    for a full recovery.
:::

::: notes
The third bullet is the one to stop on.

*[reveal to the third bullet]*

Depositors are unsure *which* banks are insolvent. Not that the banks are
insolvent - that they cannot tell which.

*[ask]* Why does a panic hit good banks as well as bad ones?

Because the depositor cannot tell them apart. That is adverse selection, in a
queue outside a branch. And it is exactly what deposit insurance was invented to
stop, which is section five.

*[the fourth bullet]*

Then the fire sale. Selling assets quickly to raise cash drives the price down,
which worsens the balance sheet of every other institution holding the same
asset. A bank acting prudently makes its neighbour insolvent.

*[the last bullet]*

Years, not quarters. Worth saying, because the recovery is the part people
forget when they imagine regulation can simply be undone.
:::

## 1 · Stage three of debt deflation

If the crisis also leads to a **sharp decline in prices**, debt deflation can
occur: asset prices fall, but **debt levels do not adjust**, increasing debt
burdens.

::: incremental
-   This leads to an increase in adverse selection and moral hazard, followed by
    decreased lending.
-   Economic activity remains depressed for a **long time**.
:::

::: notes
Short, and make the mechanism concrete with a number.

Debt is written in nominal terms. The price level falls by a quarter; your debt
does not fall at all.

*[ask]* You owe a hundred and prices fall twenty-five per cent. What has
happened to what you owe, in real terms?

It has risen by a third, without you borrowing another penny. That is debt
deflation, and it is why the Great Depression was so much worse than anything
since.

Note what it requires: a sharp fall in the *price level*, not in asset prices.
That is why stage three does not always happen - 2008 had falling asset prices
but no general deflation.
:::

::: {.content-visible when-format="beamer"}

**Three triggers:** deterioration in financial institutions' balance sheets; an
asset-price decline; an increase in uncertainty.

**Stage one — initiation.** Adverse selection and moral hazard problems worsen
and lending contracts.

**Stage two — banking crisis.** Economic activity declines, producing a banking
crisis, which worsens the information problem again.

**Stage three — debt deflation.** An unanticipated decline in the price level
worsens it a third time, and activity stays depressed.

:::

::: notes
This is the chapter's own diagram, redrawn. Walk it left to right and do not let
them write while you do it.

*[the three triggers]*

Everything we have just done, in one picture: deterioration in balance sheets,
an asset-price decline, or an increase in uncertainty.

*[stage one]*

All three arrive at the same place - adverse selection and moral hazard worsen,
and lending contracts.

*[stage two]*

Economic activity declines, which produces a banking crisis, which worsens the
information problem again, which reduces activity further. Point at the loop: it
feeds itself.

*[stage three]*

And if there is an unanticipated decline in the price level, the loop runs a
third time.

*[the caption]*

The same box appears at every stage - adverse selection and moral hazard worsen,
and lending contracts. One mechanism, three stages. If they take one picture
from this session, this is the one.
:::

# 2 · The Great Depression {.divider .center background-color="#06302F"}

## 2 · Monetary policy and agriculture

::: incremental
-   In 1928 and 1929, stock prices **doubled** in the US. The Fed tried to curb
    the speculation with a tight monetary policy — but this led to a market
    collapse of more than **20%** in October 1929, and another 20% by the year's
    end. The decline continued for several years.
-   What might have been a normal recession became far worse when severe
    **droughts** in 1930 in the Midwest led to a sharp decline in agricultural
    production.
-   Between 1930 and 1933, **one-third of US banks** went out of business as
    these agricultural shocks led to bank failures.
-   For more than two years, the Fed **sat idly by** through one bank panic
    after another. Adverse selection and moral hazard became severe, and firms
    with productive uses of funds were unable to get financing.
-   Credit spreads increased from **2%** to nearly **8%** during the height of
    the Depression in 1932.
:::

::: notes
Two shocks, and the second is the one they will not expect.

*[first bullet]*

Prices doubled in two years. The Fed tightened deliberately to stop the
speculation, and the market fell by more than forty per cent across the autumn.

*[ask]* Was tightening a mistake?

Keep it short and honest: it was aimed at a real problem and worked far better
than intended. What turned a bad recession into the worst crisis in American
history was what came next.

*[second and third bullets]*

Drought. An agricultural shock, in an economy where banks lent to farmers. One
third of American banks gone in three years.

*[fourth and fifth]*

And the Fed did nothing for two years. Connect it back to the sequence: the
system lost the institution that evaluates borrowers, so good firms could not
borrow. The spread from two per cent to eight is that sentence with a number
attached.
:::

## 2 · Credit spreads during the Depression

```{r}
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 4.3
baa <- fred("BAA")
ltg <- fred("LTGOVTBD")
if (is.null(baa) || is.null(ltg)) {
  no_data_note("BAA / LTGOVTBD")
} else {
  d <- merge(baa, ltg, by = "date")
  d$spread <- d$value.x - d$value.y
  d <- d[!is.na(d$spread) &
         d$date >= as.Date("1929-01-01") & d$date <= as.Date("1939-12-01"), ]
  pk <- d[which.max(d$spread), ]
  ggplot(d, aes(date, spread)) +
    geom_line(colour = IF_COL$teal700, linewidth = .7) +
    geom_point(data = pk, colour = IF_COL$clay, size = 2.8) +
    annotate("text", x = pk$date, y = pk$spread + .5, hjust = 0.1,
             label = sprintf("peak %.1f points, %s", pk$spread,
                             format(pk$date, "%B %Y")),
             colour = IF_COL$clay, size = 3.9) +
    labs(x = NULL, y = "Percentage points",
         title = "Credit spreads during the Great Depression",
         subtitle = "Moody's Baa corporate yield less the long-term US government yield",
         caption = "Source: Moody's and NBER long-term government bond yields, via FRED.") +
    theme_if()
}
```

::: notes
One chart, one sentence, and the sentence is the hook slide coming back.

*[point at the level before 1931]*

About two points. That is the normal price of lending to a decent but not
perfect borrower.

*[then the peak]*

Then the peak in 1932. The spread is the compensation a lender demands for not
being sure. It did not widen because firms suddenly became four times worse - it
widened because nobody could tell which firms were which.

*[ask]* If you ran a sound business in 1932 and needed to borrow, what had
changed about you?

Nothing. You simply could not prove it. That is a crisis as an information
event, measured in percentage points.

*[the chapter also shows a stock price chart here]*

The source deck has the Dow indexed to September 1929 alongside this, falling to
about a tenth of its peak by December 1932. That series is not freely available,
so quote the number rather than showing it: the market lost roughly ninety per
cent.

*[if the chart has not rendered]*

It needs the FRED series BAA and LTGOVTBD in the cache - the long-term
government yield is a discontinued series covering 1919 to 2000, which is why it
is not the GS10 used later.
:::

## 2 · The consequences

::: incremental
-   The deflation during the period led to a **25%** decline in price levels.
-   The prolonged contraction led to an unemployment rate around **25%**.
-   The Depression was the **worst financial crisis ever** in the US.
-   Bank panics in the US spread to the rest of the world, and the contraction
    of the US economy decreased demand for foreign goods.
-   The worldwide depression caused great hardship, and the resulting discontent
    led to the **rise of fascism and the Second World War**.
:::

::: notes
Short, and do not rush the last line.

Twenty-five per cent deflation - that is stage three, debt deflation, in the
data. Debts were fixed in nominal terms and everything else fell, so real
burdens rose by a quarter.

Twenty-five per cent unemployment.

*[the international bullets]*

The panic was American and the depression was global, through two channels:
banking contagion, and the collapse in American demand for everyone else's
exports.

*[the last bullet - deliver it plainly and stop]*

The chapter says it and it is right to say it. Do not editorialise. Let it land
and move on.

This is also the answer to anyone who asks why financial regulation gets the
attention it does.
:::

# 3 · The Global Financial Crisis {.divider .center background-color="#06302F"}

## 3 · Three central factors

:::: columns
::: {.column width="34%"}
**Financial innovation in mortgage markets**

Less-than-creditworthy borrowers could buy homes through **subprime lending**, a
practice almost nonexistent until the 2000s.

Financial engineering developed new products to further enhance and distribute
the risk from mortgage lending.
:::

::: {.column width="33%"}
**Agency problems**

Originators did not hold the mortgage; they **sold the note** in the secondary
market.

They earned fees on the **volume** of loans, not the quality. In the extreme,
unqualified borrowers bought houses through creative products or outright fraud
— inflated income.
:::

::: {.column width="33%"}
**Asymmetric information in the rating process**

Agencies **consulted** with firms on structuring products to achieve the highest
rating — a clear conflict.

The rating system was not designed for the complex nature of structured debt.
The result was meaningless ratings that investors had relied on.
:::
::::

::: {.source}
[A short film on what the mortgage chain looked like from the inside](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=GPOv72Awo68)
:::

::: notes
Three columns, one point each, and the middle one is the heart of it.

*[innovation]*

Subprime barely existed before the 2000s. Financial engineering then sliced and
redistributed the risk - which is the next slide.

*[agency problems - spend the time here]*

Set up the chain before you explain it: a borrower, an originator, a bank that
buys the note, a special purpose vehicle, a rating agency, and an investor.

*[ask]* Go along that chain. Who loses money if the borrower cannot pay?

The investor at the end - and nobody else, at least not quickly. The originator
has been paid and has moved on.

So the person closest to the borrower, the only one who could verify anything,
has no stake in whether the loan is repaid. Then ask what they would expect to
happen to lending standards, and let them answer.

*[rating agencies]*

Paid by the issuer, advising on structure, rating the result. They met that
exact structure last session as a conflict of interest. Say so, and say this is
what it looks like at scale.
:::


:::

::: {.content-visible when-format="beamer"}

A special purpose vehicle buys a pool of assets and issues tranches defined by
default priority. From the bottom: the **equity** tranche takes the first loss;
then **mezzanine**, with more risk and higher interest; then **senior**; then
**super senior**, last to suffer any loss. Losses fill upwards; the interest
paid falls as you move up.

:::

::: ask
What are the **risks** linked to CDOs?
:::

::: notes
Five minutes in pairs after you have walked the picture, then collect.

*[walk the diagram first]*

A special purpose vehicle buys assets, creates securities from them, and sells
those securities. The securities are tranches, defined by default priority. The
first defaults hit the lowest tranche; the highest tranches suffer only if most
of the assets default.

From the bottom: equity takes the first loss; mezzanine next, with more risk and
higher interest; then senior; then super senior.

*[then collect the risks - expect three and push for the fourth]*

Correlation. The whole structure assumes defaults are largely independent. If
they are correlated - and in a national housing downturn they are - losses do
not stay in the bottom tranches, and the senior tranches fail too. That is the
risk the ratings missed.

Opacity and valuation. Nobody could value these in a hurry, which is what froze
the market: not that they were worthless, but that nobody could show they were
not.

Model and rating risk. The rating was produced by the agency that helped
structure the deal, using models not built for the product.

Liquidity. They were held with short-term funding, so a fall in value forced
sales, which forced the value down further.

*[and the structural one, if they get there]*

Tranching does not reduce the total risk of the pool. It redistributes it. The
pool is exactly as risky as it was; what changed is who holds which part - and
how safe the top part was allowed to look.

**Worked.** Correlation of defaults breaks the tranching; opacity makes
valuation impossible; ratings were conflicted and model-driven; short-term
funding forced fire sales. Tranching redistributes risk, it does not reduce it.
:::

## 3 · US residential housing

::: incremental
-   Initially, the housing boom was **lauded** by economists and politicians,
    and it helped stimulate growth in the subprime market as well.
-   However, underwriting standards fell and people were clearly buying houses
    they could not afford — except for the ability to **sell at a higher price**.
-   Lending standards allowed near **100% financing**, so owners had little to
    lose by defaulting when the bubble burst.
-   Because of the fall in US housing prices, the number of **defaults**
    continued to plague the US banking system.
:::

::: notes
The third bullet is the one to dwell on, because it is moral hazard with a
number.

*[first two bullets, briskly]*

Rising homeownership was a policy success before it was a crisis, which is worth
saying - nobody set out to cause this.

Underwriting standards fell. The loan only worked if the house kept rising,
which is not lending, it is a bet on an asset price.

*[third bullet - stop here]*

Near one hundred per cent financing means the buyer has almost no equity.

*[ask]* You put in nothing and the house falls twenty per cent. What do you lose
by walking away?

Almost nothing. That is moral hazard in debt, exactly as we drew it last
session: the borrower keeps the upside and the lender takes the downside. The
down payment was never about affordability - it was the borrower's stake in not
defaulting.
:::

## 3 · Housing prices

```{r}
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 4.3
hp <- fred("SPCS20RSA")
if (is.null(hp)) {
  no_data_note("SPCS20RSA")
} else {
  hp <- hp[!is.na(hp$value) &
           hp$date >= as.Date("2002-01-01") & hp$date <= as.Date("2009-12-01"), ]
  hp$value <- hp$value / max(hp$value) * 100
  pk <- hp[which.max(hp$value), ]
  tr <- hp[which.min(hp$value), ]
  ggplot(hp, aes(date, value)) +
    geom_line(colour = IF_COL$teal700, linewidth = .8) +
    geom_point(data = rbind(pk, tr), colour = IF_COL$clay, size = 2.8) +
    annotate("text", x = pk$date, y = pk$value + 2.5, hjust = 0.5,
             label = paste("peak,", format(pk$date, "%B %Y")),
             colour = IF_COL$clay, size = 3.9) +
    annotate("text", x = tr$date, y = tr$value - 3.2, hjust = 0.6,
             label = sprintf("down %.0f%% from the peak", 100 - tr$value),
             colour = IF_COL$clay, size = 3.9) +
    labs(x = NULL, y = "Index, peak = 100",
         title = "Housing prices and the financial crisis of 2007–2009",
         subtitle = "S&P/Case-Shiller 20-city composite, rebased to its own peak",
         caption = "Source: S&P Dow Jones Indices via FRED.") +
    theme_if()
}
```

::: notes
This is the slide that makes the rest of the section inevitable.

*[the shape]*

Four years up, then down. Nothing unusual about a cycle - what matters is what
was built on top of it.

*[ask]* Every mortgage in those CDOs was secured on one of these houses. So what
does this chart do to the senior tranches?

It is the correlation answer from Problem 4.1, arriving as data. When house
prices fall nationally, defaults are not independent events happening to
unlucky people - they are one event happening to everybody at once, so losses go
straight through the equity tranche and keep going.

*[the near-100% financing point]*

And remember the buyer who put nothing down. At this depth of fall, enormous
numbers of borrowers owed more than the house was worth, with no equity to lose
by walking away.
:::

## 3 · The Fed

:::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
**The charge**

The Fed was blamed by some for the housing price bubble. Some argue that low
interest rates from **2003 to 2006** fuelled it — rates below what the **Taylor
rule** implied.
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**The rebuttal**

In early 2010 Bernanke rebutted this argument, saying rates were appropriate.
He pointed instead to new mortgage products, relaxed lending standards and
capital inflows as more likely causes.
:::
::::

::: {.source}
The debate over whether monetary policy was to blame for the housing price
bubble continues.
:::

::: notes
*[first to cut if you are behind]*

Two minutes, presented as an open question, because it is one.

The charge: rates were too low for too long by the standard of a simple rule,
and cheap money inflated house prices.

The rebuttal, from the chairman at the time: rates were appropriate, and the
causes were the products, the standards and the global capital inflows.

*[ask]* How would you tell which is right?

That is the useful part of this slide. You would want countries with different
monetary policies and similar housing booms, or the reverse. Several European
countries had booms without the Fed's rates. It does not settle it, but it tells
them what evidence would look like - which is worth more than the answer.
:::

## 3 · Financial institutions and firms

::: incremental
-   As mortgage defaults rose, banks and other institutions saw the value of
    their assets fall — complicated by the complexity of mortgages, CDOs,
    default swaps and other **difficult-to-value** assets.
-   Banks began **deleveraging**, selling assets and restricting credit, further
    depressing the struggling economy.
-   The **shadow banking system** also experienced a run: the hedge funds,
    investment banks and other liquidity providers. When short-term debt markets
    seized, so did the availability of credit to that system, leading to further
    fire sales of assets.
-   The fall in the stock market and the rise in credit spreads further weakened
    both firm and household balance sheets. Both consumption and real investment
    fell, causing a sharp contraction.
:::

::: {.source}
[A short film on the run in the shadow banking system](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0Wm6mclHyv0)
:::

::: notes
This is stage one turning into stage two, so name the stages as you go.

*[first two bullets]*

Asset values fall and cannot be verified, capital falls, lending is cut. That is
stage one, exactly as drawn.

*[third bullet - the one that needs explaining]*

The shadow banking system. Institutions doing what banks do - borrowing short
and lending long - without being banks.

*[ask]* If they are not banks, who guarantees their funding?

Nobody. No deposit insurance, no central bank window as of right. So when
short-term markets froze, they had to sell assets into a falling market.

That is a bank run, in a system with no deposits and no depositors. Say that
plainly: it is the single most useful idea on this slide.
:::

## 3 · Credit spreads

```{r}
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 4.3
baa <- fred("BAA")
gs  <- fred("GS10")
if (is.null(baa) || is.null(gs)) {
  no_data_note("BAA / GS10")
} else {
  d <- merge(baa, gs, by = "date")
  d$spread <- d$value.x - d$value.y
  d <- d[!is.na(d$spread) &
         d$date >= as.Date("2002-01-01") & d$date <= as.Date("2009-12-01"), ]
  pk <- d[which.max(d$spread), ]
  ggplot(d, aes(date, spread)) +
    geom_line(colour = IF_COL$teal700, linewidth = .8) +
    geom_point(data = pk, colour = IF_COL$clay, size = 2.8) +
    annotate("text", x = pk$date, y = pk$spread + .3, hjust = 0.9,
             label = sprintf("peak %.1f points, %s", pk$spread,
                             format(pk$date, "%B %Y")),
             colour = IF_COL$clay, size = 3.9) +
    labs(x = NULL, y = "Percentage points",
         title = "Credit spreads and the 2007–2009 financial crisis",
         subtitle = "Moody's Baa corporate yield less the 10-year Treasury yield",
         caption = "Source: Moody's and the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, via FRED.") +
    theme_if()
}
```

::: notes
Show this one beside the Depression chart if you can - the comparison is the
whole point.

*[the flat years]*

From 2002 to mid-2007 the spread sits under two points and barely moves. That is
a market that believes it can tell good borrowers from bad.

*[the spike]*

Then it goes vertical. Not because corporate America became insolvent in six
months, but because nobody knew which institutions held what.

*[ask]* Put the two charts side by side. 1932 reached about eight points, 2008
about six. Why was the outcome so much less severe the second time?

Because of everything in sections five to seven. Deposit insurance meant no
queue outside the branch. The central bank lent instead of sitting by. The
spread still tells you the information problem was severe - the difference is
what was standing underneath it.

*[the chapter also shows a stock price chart here]*

The source deck has the Dow indexed to October 2007, troughing at less than half
its peak in March 2009. Quote the number rather than showing it; the series is
not freely available.
:::

## 3 · The collapse

::: incremental
-   **Europe was first to raise the alarm.** With the downgrade of $10 billion
    in mortgage-related products, short-term money markets froze. In August 2007
    a French investment house suspended redemption of some of its money market
    funds, and banks and firms began to hoard cash.
-   The end of credit led to several bank failures. **Northern Rock** was one of
    the first, relying on short-term credit markets for funding. By most
    standards Europe experienced a more severe downturn than the US.
-   **March 2008:** Bear Stearns fails, sold to JP Morgan for 5% of its value a
    year earlier. **September 2008:** Freddie and Fannie into conservatorship;
    **Lehman Brothers** files for bankruptcy; Merrill Lynch sold to Bank of
    America at fire-sale prices; AIG experiences a liquidity crisis.
:::

::: notes
Chronology, delivered briskly. Do not let this become a war story.

*[Europe first - this is the detail worth having]*

The alarm was European, not American, and it was a money market event: a
downgrade, then a French house suspending redemptions on funds people thought
were cash. That is the money market fund problem from last session, in the wild.

*[Northern Rock]*

Funded in short-term markets rather than by deposits. When the funding stopped,
the bank stopped. Same mechanism as the shadow banking run.

*[the autumn of 2008]*

Read the list without dramatising it. The point is the speed, and that each
failure made the next more likely, because every failure increased uncertainty
about who else was exposed.

*[ask]* Which of the three triggers does that look like?

A rise in uncertainty - trigger three, feeding stage two.
:::

## 3 · The consequences

::: incremental
-   The crisis and impaired credit markets caused the **worst economic
    contraction since the Second World War**, peaking in September 2008.
    Congress passed a bailout package, but the market continued to decline and
    credit spreads reached over **500 basis points**.
-   The fall in real GDP and the increase in unemployment to over **10%** in
    2009 affected almost everyone. The recession that started in December 2007
    is now called the **Great Recession**.
-   Starting in March 2009, a bull market in stocks got under way and credit
    spreads began to fall — but the pace of the recovery was **slow**.
:::

::: notes
Short. The numbers are the content.

Five hundred basis points - that is the hook slide, closing.

*[ask]* Compare it with 1932: eight per cent spreads, twenty-five per cent
unemployment, twenty-five per cent deflation. Why was 2008 so much less severe
in the end?

The honest answer, and it sets up the second half of the session: because this
time the central bank and the government acted, and because deposit insurance
meant there was no queue outside the branch. The regulation in sections five to
seven is why 2008 was not 1932.

That is the bridge. Use it.
:::

# 4 · The European sovereign debt crisis {.divider .center background-color="#06302F"}

## 4 · Countries' difficulties {.smaller}

::: incremental
-   Up until 2007, all the countries that had adopted the euro found their
    interest rates **converging to very low levels**. At the same time, several
    were hit hard: lower tax revenue from the contraction, high expenses for
    bailouts, and fear of government default causing rates to surge.
-   **Greece was the first domino to fall.** September 2008: a projected 6%
    deficit and 100% debt-to-GDP. In October, with newly elected officials, the
    numbers were shown to be far worse. Fear of default pushed rates on Greek
    debt near **40%**, and debt-to-GDP rose to **160%** in 2012. Greece was
    forced to write down its debt — a partial default — and civil unrest broke
    out as unemployment climbed.
-   **Ireland, Portugal, Spain and Italy followed.** Governments were forced to
    embrace austerity; interest rates climbed to double digits; severe
    recessions resulted despite assurances from the ECB; and unemployment rose
    to double digits — **25% in Spain**.
:::

::: notes
*[the Greek detail is first to cut if you are behind]*

The shape of this one is a sentence: a currency union removed exchange rate risk
and markets priced the debt of very different governments as if it were the
same.

*[first bullet]*

Rates converged. Greek and German borrowing costs were nearly identical, which
with hindsight was an extraordinary thing for a market to believe.

*[ask]* What had actually been removed, and what had not?

Exchange rate risk was removed. Default risk was not - and in fact it was made
worse, because a country inside the union cannot devalue or print its own way
out.

*[second bullet]*

The detail that matters: the numbers changed when the officials changed. This
was partly an information crisis about the state of the public accounts, which
is the chapter's theme in a different market.

*[third bullet]*

Four more countries, austerity, and a quarter of Spain unemployed. Say that last
number slowly.
:::

# 5 · Asymmetric information {.divider .center background-color="#06302F"}

## 5 · Deposit insurance

Asymmetric information, moral hazard and adverse selection explain the
regulatory environment in banking.

::: incremental
-   Prior to **FDIC** insurance, bank failures meant depositors lost money, and
    "good" banks needed to separate themselves from "bad" banks.
-   The inability of depositors to assess the quality of a bank's assets can
    lead to panics — major panics in **1819, 1837, 1857, 1873, 1884, 1893,
    1907** and **1930–1933**.
-   With a government safety net, depositors will not flee the banking system at
    the first sign of trouble. Between **1934 and 1981**, fewer than **15** banks
    failed each year.
-   **Implicit** insurance is available in some countries where no explicit
    insurance organisation exists. Up to the 1960s, only **six** countries had
    deposit insurance; by the 1990s the number topped **70**.
:::

::: notes
This is the best-designed piece of regulation in the chapter, so give it its due
before the next slide takes it apart.

*[the list of panic years]*

Read them out. Eight panics in just over a century, roughly one every fifteen
years. Then: after 1934, fewer than fifteen bank failures a year for nearly half
a century.

*[ask]* What exactly did deposit insurance change?

Push past "it protected depositors". It removed the depositor's reason to run.
And since the run was what turned one bad bank into a system-wide panic, it cut
the link between an individual failure and a general collapse.

Tie it to the mechanism: the depositor could never tell a good bank from a bad
one. Insurance makes that ignorance harmless, instead of trying to cure it. That
is a different kind of solution from anything in section six, and it is why it
worked so well.
:::

## 5 · Deposit insurance effects

::: incremental
-   Explicit government insurance is associated with **less** bank sector
    stability and higher bank crises, and appears to retard financial
    development — but this appears to be only for countries with ineffective
    laws, regulation and high corruption. For emerging markets, deposit
    insurance may be the wrong medicine.
-   FDIC insurance creates **moral hazard** incentives for banks to take on
    greater risk.
-   FDIC insurance creates **adverse selection**: those who can take advantage
    of the insurance are most likely to find banks attractive.
-   **Too big to fail.** Regulators are reluctant to let the largest banks fail
    because of the potential impact on the entire system. When Continental
    Illinois failed, all deposits were insured, as were bondholders — so even
    creditors aren't interested in a bank's health. Consolidation has created
    many large banks, and banks now engage in more than just banking, extending
    FDIC cover to activities such as underwriting.
:::

::: notes
Now take it apart, and make the symmetry with the previous slide explicit.

The cure works by making the depositor indifferent. That is exactly the problem.

*[second bullet]*

Nobody is left watching the bank. The depositor was a terrible monitor, but they
were a monitor, and now they have been switched off.

*[ask]* Who is left to discipline a bank that is taking too much risk?

The regulator - which is why the rest of this section exists. Capital
requirements and supervision are the replacement for the monitoring that deposit
insurance destroyed.

*[third bullet]*

And it selects for the wrong people. The person who most wants a licence to lend
other people's insured money is precisely the person you would least like to
have one.

*[fourth bullet - Continental Illinois]*

Bondholders were protected too. So the last remaining private monitors, the
creditors, also stopped looking.
:::

## 5 · Restrictions on asset holdings

Regulations limit the type of assets banks may hold — for instance, banks may
not hold **common equity**.

::: keyidea
Even with regulations in place, the 2007–2009 global financial crisis still
occurred.
:::

::: notes
Thirty seconds, and the key idea is the whole point.

The restriction is simple: a bank may not hold common equity, because equity is
volatile and the bank is holding other people's money.

*[the key idea]*

And it did not prevent the crisis. Say that plainly rather than hurrying past
it - the restrictions were real, they were enforced, and the losses came through
assets that were permitted and highly rated. Rules bind the things you thought
of.
:::

## 5 · Capital requirements

Banks are required to hold a certain level of capital — book equity — that
depends on the type of assets the bank holds.

:::: columns
::: {.column width="52%"}
| Ratio | Definition | Minimum |
|:---|:---|---:|
| Leverage | capital ÷ total assets | **4%** |
| Core capital | core capital ÷ RWA | **8.5%** |
| Capital requirement | capital ÷ RWA | **10.5%** |

::: {.smaller}
RWA = total risk-weighted assets, including off-balance-sheet activities. New
capital requirements are forthcoming to address problems such as off-balance-
sheet items.
:::
:::

::: {.column width="48%"}
-   Banks engage in **regulatory arbitrage**: for a given category, they seek
    the assets that are the riskiest.
-   An undercapitalised bank is more likely to fail *and* more likely to engage
    in risky activities — so the **FDIC Improvement Act of 1991** requires the
    FDIC to act quickly.
-   "Well capitalised" banks are permitted some underwriting risk;
    "undercapitalised" banks are subject to greater reporting requirements and
    regulatory oversight.
:::
::::

::: notes
The three ratios are the examinable content. Get the difference between them
straight before the problem.

Leverage ratio: capital over total assets. It does not care what the assets are.

The other two are over risk-weighted assets, where each asset is multiplied by a
weight reflecting its risk. Capital over risk-weighted assets, and a stricter
version using only core capital.

*[ask]* Why have both a leverage ratio and a risk-weighted one?

Because each catches what the other misses. The leverage ratio is blind to risk,
so a bank can satisfy it while holding nothing but risky assets. The
risk-weighted ratio depends on the weights being right - and the crisis showed
they were not.

*[regulatory arbitrage - the key idea of the slide]*

Within a weight category, every asset counts the same. So pick the riskiest one
in the bucket. You are not breaking the rule; you are being paid to find its
edges. Every quantitative rule has this property and it is worth naming.
:::

## 5 · Problem 4.2 — First National Bank {.smaller}

:::: columns
::: {.column width="56%"}
| Assets | | Liabilities | |
|:---|---:|:---|---:|
| Reserves | $3m | Checkable deposits | $27m |
| Treasury securities | $10m | Nontransactions deposits | $65m |
| Government agency securities | $7m | Borrowings | $19m |
| Municipal bonds | $10m | Loan loss reserves | $2m |
| Residential mortgages | $10m | Bank capital | $7m |
| Real estate loans | $20m | | |
| Commercial & industrial loans | $35m | | |
| Fixed assets | $5m | | |
| Letters of credit | $20m | | |
:::

::: {.column width="44%"}
**Risk weights**

-   **0** — reserves, Treasury securities
-   **0.2** — government agency securities
-   **0.5** — municipal bonds, residential mortgages
-   **1.0** — real estate loans, C&I loans, fixed assets, letters of credit

::: ask
1.  Is the **leverage ratio** respected?
2.  Are the **core capital** and **capital requirement** ratios respected?
:::
:::
::::

::: notes
Ten minutes in pairs. This is the only arithmetic in the chapter and it is the
obvious exam question, so do not cut it and do not rush it.

*[step one - total assets]*

Add the asset column: 3 + 10 + 7 + 10 + 10 + 20 + 35 + 5 + 20 = 120 million.
Check it against the other side: 27 + 65 + 19 + 2 + 7 = 120. It balances.

*[step two - the leverage ratio]*

Capital over total assets: 7 over 120 = 5.83 per cent. The minimum is 4.

Passed.

*[step three - risk-weighted assets, and make them do this line by line]*

Reserves 3 times 0 is nothing. Treasuries 10 times 0, nothing.
Agencies 7 times 0.2 = 1.4.
Municipals 10 times 0.5 = 5. Residential mortgages 10 times 0.5 = 5.
Then everything at full weight: real estate 20, C&I 35, fixed assets 5, letters
of credit 20 - that is 80.

Total: 1.4 + 5 + 5 + 80 = 91.4 million.

*[step four - the two risk-weighted ratios]*

Core capital is the bank capital, 7. Over 91.4 that is 7.66 per cent, against a
minimum of 8.5. Failed.

Total capital adds the loan loss reserves: 7 + 2 = 9. Over 91.4 that is 9.85 per
cent, against a minimum of 10.5. Failed.

*[the point of the problem]*

*[ask]* The bank passes one test and fails two. How?

Because the leverage ratio does not look at what the assets are, and three
quarters of this bank's assets carry a full risk weight. A bank of Treasuries
with the same capital would pass everything.

*[ask]* How much capital does it actually need?

For the core ratio, 8.5 per cent of 91.4 is 7.77 - so about 0.77 million short.
For the total ratio, 10.5 per cent of 91.4 is 9.60 - about 0.60 short. Small
numbers, and they are still a breach.

**Worked.** Total assets 120, RWA 91.4. Leverage 7/120 = 5.83% against 4% -
passed. Core 7/91.4 = 7.66% against 8.5% - failed. Total capital 9/91.4 = 9.85%
against 10.5% - failed. Shortfalls of about 0.77m and 0.60m.
:::

# 6 · Banking regulation {.divider .center background-color="#06302F"}

## 6 · The Basel Accord

In June 1999 the Basel Committee proposed several reforms to the original Basel
Accord, with the following components:

::: incremental
-   Linking capital requirements to **actual risk** for large, international
    banks
-   Steps to strengthen the **supervisory** process
-   Increased **market discipline** mechanisms
:::

::: {.source}
Quite complex, and implementation was delayed by years. US regulators met to
determine how best to protect the FDIC insurance fund under the new
requirements. Only the largest US banks were subject to Basel 2; others followed
a simplified standard. · [How central banks control commercial banks](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=psahnlcr-C0)
:::

::: notes
Keep this to the three pillars and the one honest observation.

Risk-based capital, supervision, market discipline. Those are the three legs,
and they map onto the three things a regulator can do: set a rule, look at the
bank, or make the bank tell everyone else what it is doing.

*[the source line - say it rather than skipping it]*

Complex, and delayed by years. Only the largest US banks ever came under Basel
2. That is worth saying because it is the pattern: international agreements take
so long to implement that the crisis they were designed for has often already
happened.
:::

## 6 · Basel 3

:::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
**What the 2007–2009 crisis revealed**

-   The capital required was **not enough** to weather the financial crisis
-   The weights were relying on **credit ratings**, which were unreliable
-   **Procyclical** credit standards restrict credit exactly when it is needed
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**Basel 3**, implemented by 2019

-   Quality of capital
-   Less procyclical
-   New credit rating rules
:::
::::

::: notes
The left column is the examinable half, and the third item is the deepest.

*[first two]*

Not enough capital, and the weights depended on ratings that turned out to be
worthless. Both are failures of calibration rather than of principle.

*[procyclicality - stop here]*

This one is a failure of design, and they met it last session.

*[ask]* A downturn starts, losses arrive, capital falls. What does the rule
require the bank to do?

Rebuild capital - which means raising equity in a falling market, or shrinking
lending. Every bank does it at the same time, so credit is withdrawn from the
economy precisely when the economy most needs it.

The rule designed to make each bank safe makes the system more fragile.
Individually prudent, collectively destructive.
:::

## 6 · Financial supervision

::: incremental
-   Financial supervision is used to reduce the **adverse selection** problem of
    risk-takers.
-   **Examinations** assign a rating to a bank, used to justify cease orders for
    risky activities.
-   There is **periodic reporting** and frequent examination to assess the
    financial situation.
-   Banks can be declared a **"problem bank"** and subjected to more frequent
    examinations.
:::

::: notes
Two minutes. The framing in the first bullet is the part worth saying out loud.

Supervision exists to reduce an adverse selection problem: banking attracts
risk-takers, and you cannot tell them apart from the outside. So you look.

*[the rest]*

Examinations produce a rating, the rating justifies an order to stop doing
something, and a bad enough rating puts you on a list and brings the examiners
back more often.

*[ask]* Who is the supervisor standing in for?

The depositor, who stopped watching once the deposits were insured. Every item
on this slide is the public doing the monitoring that the private monitor no
longer has a reason to do.
:::

## 6 · Assessment of risk management

Past examinations focused primarily on the **quality of assets**; the new trend
focuses on whether the bank may take **excessive risk in the near future**.

::: incremental
-   Quality of **board and senior management** oversight
-   Adequacy of **policies** limiting risk activity
-   Quality of risk **measurement and monitoring**
-   Adequacy of **internal controls** to prevent fraud
:::

::: {.source}
US regulators have adopted similar guidelines for interest-rate risk.
Particularly important is the implementation of **stress testing** and
calculations to measure potential losses.
:::

::: notes
*[first to cut if you are behind]*

The shift in focus is the thing to notice.

Examinations used to ask whether the assets were good. Now they ask whether the
bank is the kind of institution that will take excessive risk next year.

*[ask]* Why the change?

Because asset quality is backward-looking. By the time the assets are visibly
bad it is too late. The four elements are all about process and people rather
than holdings.

*[stress testing]*

And stress testing is the formal version of the same idea: not what are you
worth today, but what would you be worth if things went badly.
:::

## 6 · Disclosure requirements

::: incremental
-   Better information reduces **both** moral hazard and adverse selection.
-   **Sarbanes-Oxley** increased requirements for accurate accounting statements
    and put limits on conflicts of interest.
-   If asset values can be determined, **mark-to-market** accounting may help.
:::

::: notes
Short - the fuller treatment of mark-to-market is two slides further on.

Disclosure is the purest information remedy in the chapter: it attacks the
problem directly rather than working around it. If the difficulty is that nobody
can tell who is sound, make everyone say.

*[Sarbanes-Oxley]*

Two things at once: accurate statements, and limits on conflicts of interest.
Both of those are session six arriving in law.

*[the third bullet]*

Note the conditional - *if* asset values can be determined. That qualification
is the whole of the mark-to-market slide later, so plant it here and move on.
:::

## 6 · Consumer protection

::: incremental
-   Interest rates are **standardised** — the APR — and standardisation helps
    prevent discrimination.
-   The 2007–2009 crisis revealed further need for consumer protection, as
    consumers took out loans whose terms they clearly did not understand. During
    the boom, originators had little incentive to ensure subprime borrowers could
    repay. One infamous mortgage was dubbed the **NINJA** loan: no income, no
    job, no assets.
-   In July 2008 the Federal Reserve addressed some issues for subprime loans:
    mortgages had to consider **ability to repay**; no-doc loans were banned;
    prepayment penalties were banned; escrow accounts were required.
-   A new **consumer financial protection agency** took responsibility for most
    financial products used by a typical consumer.
:::

::: notes
Begin with why standardisation is regulation at all, because it looks trivial.

*[first bullet]*

The APR exists so that two offers can be compared. Without a common definition
the consumer cannot compare, and if they cannot compare they cannot choose - so
competition does not discipline anybody. A disclosure rule is a competition
policy.

*[second bullet]*

NINJA. No income, no job, no assets. Say it once, let them laugh, then ask the
serious question.

*[ask]* Who, in that transaction, was behaving irrationally?

Arguably nobody. The borrower got a house with no money down. The originator got
a fee and sold the note. The buyer of the note held a rated security. Each link
behaved sensibly; the chain was insane. That is an incentive failure, as against
a stupidity failure.

*[third and fourth bullets, briskly]*

The 2008 rules are all one idea: put the obligation to check back on the person
making the loan.
:::

## 6 · Restrictions on competition

::: incremental
-   **Branching restrictions** reduce competition between banks.
-   **Separation of banking and securities** industries prevented nonbanks from
    competing with banks — repealed in **1999**.
-   Less competition can lead to **higher fees and less innovation**.
:::

::: notes
*[first to cut if you are behind]*

One minute. The shape is a trade-off, so say it as one.

Restricting competition makes banks safer, because a bank with a protected
market has something to lose and will not gamble it. And it makes banking worse,
because protected firms charge more and innovate less.

*[the 1999 repeal]*

Most of those restrictions have now gone. Whether removing them mattered is
argued about to this day, and it is the backdrop to every conflict of interest
we met last session.
:::

## 6 · Macro versus microprudential regulation

::: incremental
-   **Micro** regulation focuses on individual banks, but it is not enough in a
    financial crisis.
-   **Macro** regulation looks at the banking system as a whole: the **leverage
    cycle**, which feeds asset bubbles by offering more lending, can be damped;
    and a higher **net stable funding ratio** — the share of short-term funding
    in total funding — can be required.
-   Bank regulation abroad is similar to that in the US because the problems are
    similar. But international banking can readily **shift business** from one
    country to another, requiring coordination between regulators. Basel attempts
    this; these agreements do not solve all international problems.
:::

::: notes
This is the important half of the regulation section, so give it the time.

Micro-prudential regulation asks whether this bank is sound. Macro-prudential
asks whether the system is sound.

*[ask]* Can every bank be individually safe and the system still be unsafe?

Yes, and they have now seen it twice today: the procyclical capital rule, and
the fire sale where every bank selling a sound asset makes it unsound. The
fallacy of composition is the whole case for macroprudential regulation.

*[the two tools]*

The leverage cycle and the net stable funding ratio: damp the credit boom, and
make banks fund themselves with money that cannot run.

*[the international point]*

And the last bullet is why any of this is hard. If one country tightens, the
business moves. That is a regulatory version of the arbitrage from the capital
requirements slide, played at the level of countries.
:::

## 6 · E-finance and electronic banking

::: incremental
-   Electronic banking has created new issues in regulation, particularly
    **security and privacy**.
-   An incident in Russia in **1995** highlights this, where a computer
    programmer moved millions in assets from Citibank accounts to personal
    accounts.
-   It creates the need to assess the **technical skills** of banks to handle
    transactions securely and safely. **Electronic signatures** also had to be
    addressed.
-   **Privacy** is also a problem, which is why there are laws protecting
    consumers from the sharing of information — regulation likely to evolve over
    time.
:::

::: notes
*[first to cut - this is the most droppable slide in the deck]*

Two minutes if you have them, nothing if you do not.

The one idea worth leaving: a regulator supervising an electronic bank needs
technical competence, not just financial competence. The question is no longer
only whether the assets are sound but whether the systems are.

*[if the room is lively]*

*[ask]* Your bank's data is sold to an insurer who then prices your policy using
it. Which of this session's problems is that?

A conflict of interest and an information problem at once - and it is the live
regulatory question in this area now.
:::

## 6 · Mark-to-market accounting

::: incremental
-   In theory, market prices provide the **best basis** for estimating the true
    value of assets, and hence capital, in the firm.
-   But mark-to-market is subject to a major flaw: the price of an asset during
    a time of **financial distress** does not reflect its fundamental value.
-   If banks are required to show "market" value in financial records, a bank may
    appear **undercapitalised** even though prices aren't accurate.
-   The criticism was made only when asset values were **falling** (2007–2009),
    not when asset prices were booming and made balance sheets look very good
    (early 2000s).
:::

::: notes
The last bullet is the one worth the slide.

*[first three bullets]*

The principle is sound: value things at what they would fetch. And the flaw is
real: in a fire sale, the price is not the value, so a solvent bank can look
insolvent and be forced to act as though it were.

*[fourth bullet - deliver it as the observation it is]*

Notice when the objection was raised. In the boom, when market prices flattered
every balance sheet, nobody argued that market prices were unreliable.

*[ask]* Does the asymmetry mean the criticism is wrong?

No - and that is the subtle part. The argument is sound and the people making it
were not disinterested. Both can be true, and recognising it is what separates
an analyst from an advocate.
:::

# 7 · The Dodd-Frank Act {.divider .center background-color="#06302F"}

## 7 · Five different categories, July 2010 {.smaller}

::: incremental
-   **Consumer protection.** A Consumer Financial Protection Bureau is created
    to examine and enforce regulations for all businesses engaged in issuing
    financial products marketed to poor people — residential mortgage products.
-   **Resolution authority.** The US government is granted authority for
    financial firms who pose a risk to the overall financial system.
-   **Systemic risk regulation.** A Financial Stability Oversight Council is
    created to monitor markets for asset price bubbles and systemic risk,
    liquidity requirements, and the liquidation of troubled financial firms.
-   **The Volcker rule.** Banks are limited in the extent of their trading with
    their own money, and allowed to own only a small percentage of hedge and
    private equity funds.
-   **Derivatives.** Derivative products to be traded on exchanges are
    standardised, with higher capital requirements for custom products; some bank
    derivatives dealing operations are banned; and there are higher capital and
    margin requirements on firms dealing in derivatives, with more information
    about their activities.
:::

::: notes
Five categories, and each maps onto something they have already seen today. Make
that mapping explicit as you go - it is what turns a list into an argument.

Consumer protection: the NINJA loan.

Resolution authority: the answer to Lehman, where there was no orderly way to
close a large firm.

Systemic risk: the macroprudential turn, given an institution.

The Volcker rule: deposit insurance subsidises the bank's funding, so the bank
should not use that funding to speculate for its own account. That is the
too-big-to-fail subsidy being fenced off.

Derivatives: moving them onto exchanges makes positions visible, which is the
information remedy again - the AIG problem was that nobody knew who was exposed.

*[ask]* Which of the five would you expect the industry to have fought hardest?

The Volcker rule, and it is worth knowing it was substantially narrowed later.
:::

## 7 · The Too-Big-to-Fail issue

The Dodd-Frank bill does not address all areas of concern in the current
regulatory environment — the **too-big-to-fail** issue among them.

::: incremental
-   Addressing it would consist of **breaking up** large, important financial
    institutions, either by creating smaller companies out of the whole or by
    restricting asset size.
-   However, large institutions are opposed, because **synergies** in large
    institutions are eliminated, which may reduce banking efficiency.
-   **Capital requirements**, regulation and supervision of financial
    institutions are likely to be strengthened instead, to ensure they have
    enough capital to cope with the risk they take.
:::

::: notes
Two minutes, and the second bullet is the part worth being fair about.

The remedy is obvious: make them smaller, either by splitting them or by capping
their size.

*[the objection]*

And the objection is not merely lobbying. Large institutions genuinely do some
things more cheaply - a global client wants a bank that can act globally. Break
them up and you lose that.

*[ask]* So is the synergy worth the implicit guarantee that comes with being too
big to fail?

Leave it open. The point is that this is a cost-benefit question, not a morality
play, and the chapter's answer is to strengthen capital rules instead of
breaking anybody up.
:::

## 7 · Other issues

::: incremental
-   **Compensation.** Financial services pay is considered with the long-term
    effects of the compensation scheme in mind. Bonuses are paid out over a
    number of years, and only if the firm has remained in good health. Such
    **clawbacks** may encourage employees to reduce the riskiness of their
    activities.
-   **Government-sponsored enterprises.** The fate and oversight of Fannie Mae
    and Freddie Mac has not been addressed. A number of routes are available,
    each with pros and cons.
-   **Credit rating agencies.** More regulation is likely, even though
    regulation has already been strengthened to restrict conflicts of interest
    and to give incentives to provide reliable ratings.
:::

::: keyidea
More regulation is needed to prevent a crisis from ever occurring again —
although there is a substantial danger that too much, or poorly designed,
regulation could hamper the efficiency of the financial system.
:::

::: notes
Close the session on the key idea, not on the list.

*[the three open items, briskly]*

Compensation: clawbacks tie the bonus to the long-run health of the firm, which
is the principal-agent problem from last session with a contractual fix.

The GSEs and the rating agencies: both unfinished.

*[the key idea - this is the sentence to leave them with]*

Read it out. Then say what it really means: there is no setting of the dial that
is simply correct. Every rule in this session fixed an information problem and
created an incentive problem. Deposit insurance stopped the runs and switched
off the monitors. Capital rules made banks safer and made downturns deeper.
Mark-to-market told the truth and told it at the worst moment.

*[ask]* So is the right amount of regulation more, or less, than we have?

Do not answer it. Tell them that is the question the whole chapter has been
preparing them to argue, and that an answer which does not acknowledge the
trade-off is not an answer.
:::

## Next session {.center}

That completes the taught material.

::: keyidea
What remains is the **exam**. Problem 4.2 is the kind of calculation it asks;
the three stages of a crisis and the trade-off behind every regulation are the
kind of argument it asks.
:::

Pull the course together rather than listing what is next.

Four sessions ago we were pricing a bond. Then building a portfolio, then asking
why institutions exist, and today why they are regulated. The thread through all
of it is the same: finance is about valuing claims under uncertainty, and the
hard part is never the arithmetic - it is who knows what, and who has a reason
to tell you.

Tell them what the exam covers, if you have settled it.
